key_insight: Time in videos can be learned as an explicit visual concept — a compact "time‑flow" representation that lets models both recognize playback speed changes and generate the same scene at different speeds.
problem_solved: Addresses the lack of models that perceive and control the passage of time in videos: detecting whether a clip is sped up or slowed down and synthesizing speed‑changed versions while preserving semantics.
method: Self‑supervised learning from multimodal and temporal cues (visual motion, audio, scene semantics) to learn a time‑flow embedding.
Train a dual head model: one head predicts temporal rate (speed classification/regression) and the other conditions a decoder/synthesizer to produce sped‑up or slowed‑down video.
Enforce temporal‑structure and perceptual consistency (reconstruction/contrastive/consistency objectives) so speed changes preserve content and motion realism.
impact: Gives AI/ML practitioners a principled way to build temporally robust video models, perform targeted temporal data augmentation, and enable controllable video editing and synthesis workflows.
visual_elements: Triptych example: same clip at normal, sped‑up, and slowed‑down speeds (side‑by‑side comparison).
Model diagram: encoder → time‑flow embedding → (speed predictor + speed‑conditioned decoder).
Interactive speed slider illustration showing conditioning effect on output frames.
Bar chart: speed classification accuracy and qualitative realism scores vs baseline methods.
paper_title: Seeing Fast and Slow: Learning the Flow of Time in Videos
paper_authors: Yen-Siang Wu, Rundong Luo, Jingsen Zhu, Tao Tu, Ali Farhadi
